title: At-Takwir: the buried girl
hookLine: when the baby girl buried alive is asked for what sin she was killed (81:8–9)

lines: THE SUN, THE STARS, THE SEAS.
cards: Among the twelve whens of At-Takwir, the sun wrapped, the stars falling, the seas on fire, one isn't about the sky at all. It's about a single child.

Of everything the surah could show on the last day, the biggest events in the universe, it stops for one small girl whom nobody in her own world stopped for. Today's lesson is a hard one, and it's told gently.
It's about who gets to speak on that day, and who has to answer.

teach.b: Verses eight and nine, in Pickthall's words: "And when the girl-child that was buried alive is asked For what sin she was slain." Commentators say that in pre-Islamic Arabia some people killed newborn daughters.

teach.h: FEAR OF POVERTY, FEAR OF SHAME.
teach.b: The Qur'an itself names two reasons: fear of poverty, and fear of shame.

Elsewhere it describes the reaction: when one of them is told a daughter has been born, his face darkens, and he hides from people, wondering whether to keep her in humiliation or bury her in the dust.
The Qur'an forbade it outright: do not kill your children for fear of poverty. Now look at how verse nine is built.

teach.h: THE QUESTION IS PUT TO HER.
teach.b: The question isn't put to the father. It's put to her. For what sin was she killed?

Commentators notice this. The one who had no voice in her short life is the one addressed on that day, in front of everyone, and her answer will be the testimony. The question holds its own answer: no sin.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ went further than forbidding.
A hadith in Muslim's collection says that whoever raises two daughters until they grow up will come on the Day of Resurrection with him, and he held his fingers together to show how close.
He had daughters himself, and was known for standing up to greet Fatima when she came into the room.
So the surah names the harm and gives the girl the question, and the Prophet's practice turns the shame upside down: raising a daughter becomes a way to be close to him.

how: Muslims read these verses as the Qur'an's condemnation of female infanticide; the hadith on raising daughters is quoted at the birth of a girl, and the 'aqiqah, a sacrifice and a shared meal of thanks, is held for daughters as well as sons.

s: every tribe in pre-Islamic Arabia buried infant daughters
the sources describe some people doing it, not everyone; the Qur'an forbade it outright.
in 81:9 the question is put to the girl, not to her killer
commentators note the one with no voice is the one addressed.
the Prophet Muhammad had only sons
he had daughters, and was known for rising to greet his daughter Fatima.

games.q: on the last day, a question is asked about the girl who was buried alive. who is it put to?
games.why: she is asked, for what sin she was slain (81:8–9). the one silenced in life is given the question, and the answer is: none.

practice: Bring to mind a girl or woman in your life, a daughter, a sister, a niece, a mother, a student, a friend, and picture her face. Think of one thing about her that deserves to be honored out loud: her courage, her humor, her work.
If there's no one close, hold in mind girls anywhere whose lives aren't valued.

wordCard.voice: At-Takwir. The wrapping up, Surah eighty-one, where the buried girl is asked for what sin she was killed. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the girl buried alive, from w-'-d, to bury a newborn (Qur'an 81:8).
